turns.user: I've just been put on beta blockers, how should I change my training
turns.reply:
Since beta blockers blunt your heart rate, you won't be able to rely on heart rate zones or trackers to measure how hard you're working. Your heart rate simply won't go up as high, even when you are pushing maximum effort. 

Instead, you should switch entirely to using Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE) to gauge your intensity. We'll focus on how heavy the weight feels and how many reps you have left in the tank on each set, rather than what a watch says. 

Because beta blockers can also affect your blood pressure and make you feel a bit dizzy when changing positions quickly, we should be mindful of rapid transitions—like standing up quickly after a heavy squat or Romanian Deadlift. 

Since this is a new prescription, it is important to clear your training plan with your doctor or pharmacist first to ensure they are comfortable with you lifting at your usual intensity. Once they give you the green light, we can keep your sessions moving safely.

turns.user: I know you can't prescribe, just tell me roughly what to expect
turns.reply:
The main thing you'll notice is a "ceiling" on your heart rate. Even when you're working hard and breathing heavily, your heart rate won't spike the way it used to, and your fitness tracker might tell you you're barely working. That is why we rely on how many reps you have left in the tank to measure your effort.

You might also feel fatigued a bit quicker during your warm-ups or between sets, especially as your body adjusts to the medication. It can also cause a slight drop in blood pressure when you stand up quickly—so taking an extra second before walking off after a set of Romanian Deadlifts or lunges is a smart move.

Once you've had a chance to see how your body responds during your first few sessions, we can easily adjust the volume if you find you need a bit more recovery time between sets. How is your energy level feeling today?
